name: Larvikite
physical: Kept nearby for comfort in stressful times
summary: Larvikite is Norway's shimmering blue-grey igneous rock, a calming, grounding stone of stability and quiet protection in the crystal tradition.
intro: Larvikite is a coarse igneous rock, a type of monzonite, made mostly of tightly packed feldspar crystals that show a blue-silver flash across the surface. The flash is a form of schiller from thin layers inside the feldspar and is strongest in polished stone. Fresh pieces are dark grey to black with glimmering silvery blue crystals, which is why it is often marketed as Blue Pearl granite. It comes from only one famous source, the Larvik region of southern Norway, with similar material found in Brazil and elsewhere. Larvikite is heavy, tough, and shimmery, and is commonly used as a facing stone on buildings as well as in tumbled crystals.
history: Larvikite was first described in the 1880s and is named for the town of Larvik in Norway, where the Oslo Rift produced a belt of unusual igneous rocks about 290 million years ago. The stone has been quarried for a very long time and is exported worldwide as Blue Pearl or Emerald Pearl granite for kitchen countertops, building facades, and monuments. Because the stone's flash resembles moonstone, it picked up the nickname Norwegian moonstone. Norway named larvikite its national rock in 2007. In modern crystal circles, it is associated with Nordic landscapes and with the quiet, steady strength of an old mountain.
meaning: Practitioners treat larvikite as a grounding, meditative stone that quiets a busy mind. Its heavy, dark body is linked to the Root and Earth Star chakras, while its silvery flash is tied to the Third Eye and to gentle intuition. People use it when they feel scattered or anxious, saying it brings a steady, reflective mood. It is traditionally a stone for meditation, often held while sitting still in nature or by water. Larvikite is also regarded as a protective, calming stone for the home and workplace, believed to buffer stress. Some people use it in dreamwork to feel safe while exploring inner imagery. Because it is a rock rather than a single mineral, it is seen as a stone of community and collaboration.
howToUse: Hold a tumbled larvikite during seated meditation, noticing the weight and the flash in your hand. Keep a pocket stone for stressful moments, or set a slab on your desk as a steady companion. Place one at the base of a grid to anchor intuitive stones like labradorite and moonstone. A larger piece makes a nice bedside stone for evening wind-down. Wear it as a pendant or bracelet for grounded daily protection. Some people set larvikite near the front door to bring a sense of calm into the home.
care: Larvikite is Mohs 6 and quite tough as a rock, so it is easy to care for. It tolerates water, so you can rinse it under cool running water and dry it with a soft cloth. Sunlight is safe. Cleanse by moonlight, sound, smoke, or burying in earth. Avoid hard knocks, since its feldspar crystals have cleavage and can chip at edges. Store apart from harder stones. Wipe dust off polished surfaces to keep the flash bright.
identify: Genuine larvikite is dark grey with silvery blue flashing crystals that appear to float below the surface, and it feels heavy and cool in the hand. Labradorite looks similar but is a single mineral with stronger color flash. Dyed black stones may have a flat appearance without schiller. Polished slabs sold as Blue Pearl granite are the same rock as larvikite. Glass or plastic fakes lack the grainy crystalline texture visible on a broken or unpolished edge.

faq.a: Larvikite is traditionally used for grounding, calm, and meditation. Many people hold it during quiet sitting or keep it nearby to feel steady during stressful days.

faq.q: Is larvikite the same as labradorite?
faq.a: Not quite. Larvikite is a rock made mostly of feldspar, while labradorite is a single mineral. Larvikite's flash is softer and more silvery blue, while labradorite shows bright color flashes of blue, green, and gold.
Yes, larvikite is a hard, stable rock and can be rinsed under cool running water. Dry it afterward and avoid sharp knocks, because its feldspar crystals can chip along cleavage planes.
